content: The WHO Guidelines for Drinking-Water Quality, Fourth Edition (incorporating the first and second addenda, March 2022), serve as a critical reference for establishing national regulations and standards to ensure water safety and protect public health. These guidelines are updated through a rolling revision process, which allows for the periodic updating of specific sections based on new evidence, uncertainties in best practices, or stakeholder requests. Major new recommendations are typically introduced in new editions following comprehensive reviews. The latest edition emphasizes the Framework for Safe Drinking-Water, which integrates the roles of national regulators, water suppliers, and independent surveillance agencies. This framework includes the following components: 1. Development of drinking-water quality regulations and standards, including health-based targets. 2. Implementation of Water Safety Plans (WSPs), which adopt a proactive risk management approach covering all steps in the water supply chain to ensure the consistent delivery of safe and acceptable drinking water. 3. Independent surveillance to verify the effectiveness of WSPs and ensure that health-based targets are met. The guidelines are supported by a series of supplementary publications, which are referenced throughout the document. Annex 1 provides a list of these supporting publications. Key updates in the latest edition include: 1. Chemical Aspects (Chapters 8–12 and Annexes): New or updated chemical fact sheets for 14 chemicals, based on assessments from 2020 and 2021. These assessments either reaffirmed or updated guideline values, health-based values, or established reference values. New or updated fact sheets were prepared for the following chemicals: Anatoxins (new, with reference value established). Asbestos. Bentazone (acute health-based value established). Chromium (guideline value retained, provisional status removed). Cylindrospermopsins (new, with provisional guideline values for lifetime and short-term exposure established). Iodine. Manganese (provisional guideline value established, replacing the prior health-based value). Microcystins (replaces cyanobacterial toxins: microcystin-LR; short-term provisional guideline value established, provisional lifetime guideline retained). Nickel. Organotins (replaces dialkyltins; health-based value established for some organotins). Saxitoxins (new, with acute guideline value established). Silver (reference value established). Tetrachloroethene (guideline value changed). Updated tables on analytical achievability and treatment performance for cyanobacteria, cyanotoxins, and manganese (Annexes 4 and 5). 2. Radiological Aspects (Chapter 9): Updated guidance on managing radioactivity in drinking water, including recommendations for addressing radionuclides when WHO screening values and guidance levels are exceeded. Additional guidance on adapting WHO values for national regulations and on situations where the Indicative Dose Criterion (IDC) could be exceeded even if screening levels are not surpassed. 3. Cyanobacteria and Cyanotoxins: Introduction of an alert level framework for early warning and short-term management responses. This framework uses cyanobacterial biomass levels (e.g., biovolume or chlorophyll-a) to trigger responses when concentrations exceeding cyanotoxin alert values cannot be excluded. Annex 1 lists new WHO supporting publications referenced in the guidelines, including: A guide to equitable water safety planning (2019). Alternative drinking-water disinfectants: Bromine, iodine, and silver (2018). Arsenic primer: Guidance on investigating and mitigating arsenic contamination (2018). Chemical mixtures in source water and drinking water (2017). Climate-resilient water safety plans (2017). Developing drinking-water quality regulations and standards (2018). Domestic water quantity, service level, and health, 2nd edition (2020). Management of radioactivity in drinking water (2018). Microplastics in drinking water (2019). Potable reuse: Guidance for producing safe drinking water (2017). These updates reflect the WHO's commitment to ensuring safe drinking water through evidence-based recommendations and comprehensive guidance.
